evidence.title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Multidisciplinary governance review of model inputs and clinician interpretability changed the deployed model design
evidence.effect: Expert review raised concern about clinicians interpreting race as a predictor, and this fed into selecting fairness through blindness as the revised model.
evidence.quote: More importantly, it meets the expert feedback highlighting the difficulties clinicians might face interpreting race as a top predictor in a clinical decision support tool.

evidence.title: Dosimetric Impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Based Autocontouring Software, OncoStudio, in High-Risk Prostate Cancer Treatment Planning: A Three-Group Comparative Study on the Slice Ranges of Seminal Vesicles
evidence.outcome: Effect of adjusting AI seminal vesicle contours to institutional guideline on dose agreement with manual
evidence.effect: Adjusted AC gave distributions closer to manual contouring; effect sizes g=0.53-0.63 versus g=0.67-0.78 for unadjusted AC; none statistically significant.
evidence.quote: The adjusted AC group showed distribution characteristics closer to those of the MC group, supporting the effectiveness of SV area adjustment.

evidence.title: Using large language models to enhance clinically-driven missing data recovery algorithms in electronic health records
evidence.outcome: Clinician validation of LLM-generated clinical knowledge (search terms) before use
evidence.effect: Clinicians removed 18% of LLM (context) matched codes not clinically relevant; the clinician-approved roadmap recovered 73 (18%) missing values vs 83-89 (20-22%) for unreviewed LLM roadmaps.
evidence.quote: Large language models (context + clinicians) recovered more than the experts but less than the LLMs alone (73, 18 % ), suggesting that the enhancements successfully broadened the search terms but not all were clinically relevant.

evidence.title: Initial specialist validation of clinical decision support recommendations from a machine learning-enabled digital cognitive assessment
evidence.outcome: Specialist neurologist appropriateness ratings of AI-linked CDS recommendations and pathways (median >=7 threshold)
evidence.effect: All cognitive-impairment recommendations met the threshold; all seven borderline/impaired-DCR pathways appropriate (median 7-8); two pathways fell below threshold (Green DCR median 6; anti-amyloid referral median 5).
evidence.quote: All cognitive-impairment recommendations met the threshold.
evidence.sample_unit: de-identified patient reports rated by 5 neurologists

evidence.title: An LLM chatbot to facilitate primary-to-specialist care transitions: a randomized controlled trial
evidence.effect: Locally fine-tuned PreA omitted needed diagnoses in 30.0% (90 of 300) and testing suggestions in 39.3% (118 of 300) simulated cases.
evidence.quote: Mirroring real-world clinician patterns, the data-tuned model exhibited suboptimal adherence to diagnostic guidelines, failing to provide diagnoses (30.0%, 90 of 300) or suggest testing (39.3%, 118 of 300) when needed.

evidence.title: Dosimetric Impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Based Autocontouring Software, OncoStudio, in High-Risk Prostate Cancer Treatment Planning: A Three-Group Comparative Study on the Slice Ranges of Seminal Vesicles
evidence.effect: Unadjusted AC included entire SVs; CTV Dmean -58.7 cGy (0.8%) and PTV Dmean -92.8 cGy vs MC, within clinically acceptable ranges.

evidence.title: Cultural bias in large language models' ability to follow neuroradiology guidelines
evidence.outcome: Adherence of LLM imaging recommendations to non-US vs US guidelines when explicitly instructed
evidence.effect: Explicit setting: DeepSeek 86.7% US vs 30.0% non-US (p<0.001); GPT-o3 76.7% vs 36.7% (p=0.004); Mistral 80.0% vs 30.0% (p<0.001).
evidence.quote: All three models performed significantly better when the guideline originated from the U.S. than on non-U.S. guidelines.

evidence.title: AI-assisted VMAT planning incorporating deep learning-based dose prediction for head and neck cancer: feasibility of quality standardization and human intervention for irregular cases
evidence.venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
evidence.effect: Vendor-recommended initial AI plans exceeded local maximum-dose tolerance in three cases.
evidence.quote: Conversely, the initially calculated AI‐assisted plans using the vendor‐recommended optimization parameters exhibited a tendency toward an elevated maximum dose near the body surface, exceeding our institution's tolerance in three cases.

evidence.effect: Operational workflows were the majority of LLM errors, rather than medical knowledge alone.

evidence.title: Comparison of Vendor-Pretrained and Custom-Trained Deep Learning Segmentation Models for Head-and-Neck, Breast, and Prostate Cancers
evidence.effect: Vendor breast contours excluded pectoralis major and retracted from skin, unlike local institutional practice; custom contours aligned with local 3D CRT practice.
evidence.quote: In contrast, the vendor-pretrained model adheres to guidelines that exclude the pectoralis major, and the breast contour is retracted from the skin to accommodate dose buildup within the breast in Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT) [ Figure 2 (Case 3-A1, Case 4-C1)].

commentary.bottom_line: Four small offline studies suggest that clinical expert review before deployment can find and correct AI content that conflicts with local guidelines, clinical relevance, or clinician interpretation, but none measured effects on patient outcomes in live use. Eleven hazard studies show that AI outputs often diverge from local guidelines and practice, which supports the need for the safeguard without showing how well it works.

perspectives.view: All four tests of the practice are level 4 retrospective replays with raters in offline settings, with samples from 15 to 1000 patients plus one cohort of 55,303 deliveries. Results point in the same direction, but the outcomes are process measures, one contouring effect was not statistically significant, and no study used a concurrent control. Certainty is very low.

Clinician review removed 18% of LLM-matched codes as not clinically relevant, and five neurologists rated two AI-linked pathways below the appropriateness threshold (medians 6 and 5). These results suggest that review catches some errors before use. Hazard studies report omitted diagnoses in 30.0% of simulated cases and physician rejection of 7 of 15 recommendations for deviating from national TB guidelines.

Adjusting AI seminal vesicle contours to the institutional guideline brought dose distributions closer to manual contouring (g=0.53-0.63 versus 0.67-0.78), though no difference reached significance. Hazard studies found that operational workflow problems made up most LLM errors and that only 19% of AI order set suggestions were useful. No test reported reviewer time or burden.

Multidisciplinary review in a 55,303-delivery obstetric cohort raised concern that clinicians would read race as a predictor, and the team moved to a race-blind model. In non-English settings, LLMs followed non-US imaging guidelines in 30.0% to 36.7% of vignettes versus 76.7% to 86.7% for US guidelines, which suggests local validation may matter more outside US contexts.

Six sources endorse expert validation, and three of them, including the CHAI assurance guide, state it as a requirement. One guidance document calls for human examination of patient records before a care denial. None of the supplied studies tests whether meeting these expectations changes compliance or outcomes.

Vendor defaults conflicted with local practice in several radiation oncology studies. Vendor-recommended plans exceeded local maximum-dose tolerance in three of 12 cases, 9 of 10 radiation oncologists said auto-segmented targets differed from their routine practice, and vendor breast contours departed from institutional conventions. No study reported the staffing or cost needed to perform expert validation.

Patient-facing content showed local mismatches, with one model citing US resources in 57.1% of responses to Caribbean patients and faculty judging 40% of AI-generated consent forms unfit for Indian use. No test of expert validation examined patient-facing content, so its effect on what patients read and whom they can contact is unknown.

commentary.research_gap: No prospective or real-deployment study has compared AI tools with and without pre-deployment expert validation on the rate of guideline-discordant outputs reaching clinicians or patients, on downstream patient outcomes, or on the reviewer time and cost involved. Studies of patient-facing tools and administrative uses such as care denials are also absent.
commentary.underserved_note: The four tests of the practice included a racial and ethnic minority focus in one study and older adults in another, but none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Hazard studies documented local mismatches in limited English proficiency, low-literacy, low-income, and rural populations, so the practice remains untested where the hazard has been shown to occur.
